analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to count drug copay assistance and other aid toward patients' deductibles and out-of-pocket limits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite 25 cosponsors from both parties, when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Many health plans use what are called 'copay accumulator' rules: when a drug maker, charity, or someone else helps a patient pay a copay or deductible, the plan does not count that help toward the patient's deductible or yearly out-of-pocket maximum. The patient still owes the full amount themselves, even though money was paid on their behalf. This bill would require plans to count that assistance — including third-party payments, financial assistance, discounts, and product vouchers — toward deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who receive help paying for their care — most commonly copay cards from drug manufacturers or aid from charitable foundations — would see that money actually reduce their out-of-pocket burden. Under current accumulator practices, a patient can receive thousands of dollars in assistance and still hit their full deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, paying the entire amount themselves once the assistance runs out. Counting assistance toward those limits means patients reach their out-of-pocket maximum sooner and stop paying.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to count amounts paid by or on behalf of an enrollee — including third-party payments, financial assistance, discounts, product vouchers, and other reductions in out-of-pocket expenses — toward deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket limits.
Applies to group health plans and to group and individual health insurance coverage, amending the Public Health Service Act and conforming the Affordable Care Act's cost-sharing provisions.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and group health plans would bear more of patients' costs, since assistance that currently lets them collect patient cost-sharing without reducing patients' burden would instead have to count toward patients' limits. Those costs would flow partly into premiums. Drug makers that fund copay cards would also see their assistance become a more effective tool for keeping patients on their brand-name drugs rather than cheaper generics.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and group health plans

drawbacks.text: Plans and employers argue that counting outside assistance toward cost-sharing limits raises claims costs, which flows into premiums for everyone — meaning patients who receive no assistance effectively subsidize those who do.

The bill does not address why patients need help affording drugs in the first place: manufacturer copay cards can steer patients toward expensive brand-name drugs over cheaper generics, so the bill could entrench a mechanism that keeps overall drug prices high.
The bill mandates counting of assistance but does nothing to require that assistance exist or reach the patients who need it, leaving the underlying affordability problem in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing high cost-sharing, the direct benefit is real and immediate: money paid on their behalf would finally count toward their limits, ending a practice where assistance effectively disappears into the plan. The honest trade-offs are that costs shift into premiums and that manufacturer copay cards, made more useful by this bill, are themselves a tool that sustains high brand-drug prices. A better-designed package would pair this with action on drug prices; on its own, it is a genuine patient-protection fix with a known cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, with Sens. Kaine, Ernst, Markey, and Murkowski as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP Committee.
The bill gathered 25 cosponsors — 16 of 48 Senate Democrats, 8 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 4 Independents — but the action history shows no further action after the referral.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and plans that benefit from not counting third-party assistance toward patients' cost-sharing limits are better off, because the practice stays legal. Patients who rely on copay assistance are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keep current copay rules

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HELP Copays Act and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Kaine, Ernst, Markey, and Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it four-way bipartisan sponsorship on day one.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its record — so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction: its five original sponsors split between two Republicans (Marshall, Ernst), two Democrats (Kaine, Markey), and Murkowski (R), and its 25 cosponsors included 16 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 Independent. There were no votes, so no recorded opposition on either side.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: Today, many plans pocket third-party assistance — like drug-maker copay cards — without counting it toward the patient's deductible or out-of-pocket maximum, so the patient still pays the full amount. The bill ends that practice, forcing plans to absorb more of patients' costs and making the assistance actually reach the patient.

Manufacturer copay cards would become more valuable, since the assistance would count toward patients' limits and keep patients able to afford brand-name drugs. But copay cards are also how drug makers steer patients away from cheaper generics and defend high list prices, so this bill strengthens that mechanism without addressing drug prices themselves.

Employers offering coverage would face higher claims costs as outside assistance must count toward employees' cost-sharing limits, likely raising premiums, though their employees who use assistance would pay less out of pocket.
